overview:
Bullying refers to repeated, intentional behavior that harms, intimidates, or coerces another person. In Jain ethical analysis, bullying is understood not only as a social and psychological harm but also as a form of himsā (violence) that generates demerit karma (pāpa). Jain traditions emphasize that violence includes physical injury, verbal aggression, emotional manipulation, and intentional humiliation. Because Jainism defines himsā as any act that causes suffering to embodied beings—whether through body, speech, or mind—bullying is treated as a serious ethical violation.

From a social perspective, bullying can occur in schools, workplaces, families, online environments, and religious communities. It often involves power imbalance, where the perpetrator uses physical strength, social status, or psychological pressure to dominate another person. Jain lay ethics (śrāvaka-ācāra) encourage nonviolence, empathy, and restraint, making bullying incompatible with the conduct expected of householders.

Modern Jain educators and community leaders often frame bullying as a contemporary challenge requiring both ethical reflection and practical intervention. While primary Jain texts do not use the modern term “bullying,” they contain extensive discussions of verbal restraint, compassion, and the avoidance of cruelty. These teachings provide a foundation for addressing bullying in youth education, family life, and community settings.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.11
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti/Umāsvāmi
primary_sources.translation: Violence consists of killing, binding, beating, overloading, terrifying, and insulting.
primary_sources.notes: This sutra is a foundational definition of himsā. The inclusion of terrifying and insulting behavior shows that verbal and emotional harm are considered forms of violence. Commentaries across traditions (Digambara and Śvetāmbara) agree that cruelty in speech and humiliation generate demerit karma.

primary_sources.title: Ācārāṅga Sūtra I.4
primary_sources.author: Attributed to Mahāvīra’s teachings; Śvetāmbara canon
primary_sources.original_text: ण वि कसायेण वि अत्तं परं वि दंसइ
primary_sources.transliteration: ṇa vi kasāyeṇa vi attaṃ paraṃ vi daṃsaï
primary_sources.translation: One should not injure oneself or others through passions.
primary_sources.notes: The text emphasizes that harm driven by anger, pride, deceit, or greed is prohibited. Bullying often arises from these passions, making this passage relevant for ethical analysis.

primary_sources.title: Dasavaikālika Sūtra 8.36
primary_sources.author: Śvetāmbara canonical text
primary_sources.notes: Although widely quoted, this line is part of a larger discussion on restraint in speech and action. It provides the overarching ethical framework within which bullying is understood as a violation.

misconceptions.reality: Jain texts classify verbal humiliation, intimidation, and emotional cruelty as forms of himsā. Bullying can be psychological, social, or digital.

misconceptions.myth: Bullying is a normal part of childhood and builds resilience.
misconceptions.reality: Jain ethics reject all forms of intentional harm. Modern psychology also shows that bullying causes long-term emotional and social damage.

misconceptions.myth: If bullying does not cause visible injury, it is not serious.
misconceptions.reality: Jainism teaches that harm through speech and intention binds karma. Emotional suffering is ethically significant even without physical wounds.
